content:
Hi all, I wanted to share a project I've been working on to help researchers from the Economics and Computation community, and broader applied modeling areas, to formalize their own research papers without knowing Lean: https://github.com/nikhgarg/EconCSLib, with project website here: https://gargnikhil.com/EconCSLib/.

This comes in two parts -- library tooling for shared concepts (especially probability, optimization, and social choice/auctions/etc), and LLM as judge auditing procedures for correct statement translation and paper coverage.

So far, I've formalized about 20 papers, including most of my relevant publications.

I'm very new to Lean and the community and I know I have a lot to learn, and would appreciate any feedback or suggestions. I see that there's a good amount of other game theory activity here by @Alex (https://github.com/alexfleetcommander/lean-proofs), @Elazar Gershuni (https://github.com/elazarg/GameTheory), @Ma, Jia-Jun (https://github.com/gametheoryinlean/EconCSLib) and potentially others as well. My understanding is that the projects are very complementary and I'd love for my project to use these other projects as trusted, upstream providers of core concepts to augment the library we're building.

As a final note, yes there are two projects called EconCSLib...the two teams have talked about it on a call; the projects are independent/concurrent and complementary, and we're figuring out potential name changes to reflect the different focuses (trusted foundations for them, modern research papers for me by authors). We'd appreciate any thoughts on name changes or other ways to navigate this as well!

formalize their own research papers without knowing Lean: https://github.com/nikhgarg/EconCSLib... So far, I've formalized about 20 papers, including most of my relevant publications.

May I ask, what exactly is the goal here? Typically, when folks do autoformalization, they at least know a little Lean to verify that their target theorem is stated correctly.

LLM as judge auditing procedures for correct statement translation and paper coverage.

LLM-as-judge is not a reliable means for verifying correct statement translation or paper coverage. There are many cases where this system has led to egregious misformalizations of the source text.

Your site describes this project as "focus[ed] on AI-assisted formalization of research papers with human-in-the-loop validation" -- can you explain what your human-in-the-loop validation system looks like? And how others can independently audit your papers?

I clicked on a random paper on your site. The PaperInterface.lean file is over 10,000 lines and completely unreadable. Yet the documentation describes this file as:

Human-Facing Paper Interface...

This is the compact Lean file a human should read after formalization to check
whether the paper's definitions and named theorem statements were represented
correctly.

Thanks Jack, I really appreciate the engagement and the feedback!

May I ask, what exactly is the goal here? Typically, when folks do autoformalization, they at least know a little Lean to verify that their target theorem is stated correctly.

Can you explain what your human-in-the-loop validation system looks like? And how others can independently audit your papers?

My goal is to achieve a higher level of confidence in my papers, as a complement to me/reviewers reading the paper carefully and an LLM without Lean going through it. In that sense, the project has started achieving its goals for my own papers -- I have found issues that have not been previously caught, and were not caught by GPT just going through the paper. I think this is valuable for my research community.

Reaching the level of confidence that we have in outputs of, say, the Mathlib project is out of scope for this project, for exactly the reasons you state (ultimately, we want human verification of all the statements, and LLM-as-Judge is fallible). I try to communicate this in the paper describing the project and in the project website (by showing a human review column), but I think I can do a better job here. I'll add this as more prominent warnings/language.

LLM-as-judge is not a reliable means for verifying correct statement translation or paper coverage. There are many cases where this system has led to egregious misformalizations of the source text.

I would agree to some extent, certainly for a level of trust we want in a Mathlib-like project. I've also observed this myself for early versions of my LLM-as-Judge approach -- important equations that needed to be formalized, that were actually incorrect, were hidden in the theorem statement as a given as opposed to actually shown. Overtime, I've substantially expanded the LLM-as-judge approach so that, in addition to holistic passes, every component of a theorem statement is extracted out and separately evaluated with its Lean translation, and all assumptions in theorem statements are traced back to a specific assumption line in the paper. Of course, this isn't perfect; ideally, as it improves, it becomes good enough to achieve the above goal.

Can you explain what your human-in-the-loop validation system looks like?

I clicked on a random paper on your site. The PaperInterface.lean file is over 10,000 lines and completely unreadable.

Thanks for pointing this out! When first starting the project, I had built a dashboard (screenshot below) so that people can compare the Lean statement to the paper statement, and mark it as verified, and it will be logged alongside their name/handle. The intention is still for this to be done, and on the website this is what the human review column refers to (with 0/X statements meaning that this hasn't been done yet).

The incongruency you point out is a consequence of developing more/stronger LLM-as-judge procedures over time. Those files started out as human facing interfaces, but overtime bloated due to the expansion of the LLM-as-judge procedures, since the row-level approach described above expanded out statements. I'm trying to think of the right way to balance a compact interface for humans, alongside having a more pedantic set that the LLM-as-judge approach can check. For now, I'll split the files.

Thanks again for the thoughts, and always happy for feedback and areas of improvement!
